terms.comment: The simple verb, of which natō is the frequentative.

terms.grammar: the supine of natō after a verb of going
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.2: vidērī vēnisse in illa loca plōrātum potius quam natātum
Hor. S. 1.5.48: lūsum it Maecēnās, dormītum ego Vergiliusque
terms.comment: Cicero’s supine of purpose: going to the bay of Naples “to swim”. Horace’s line shows the same turn with other verbs.

terms.gloss: go into the water, get in
terms.comment: Seneca’s word for getting into cold water; the lexicon says in solium dēscendere of the bath in the same way.

phrases.english: downstream you may swim too (Pliny’s rule for a river)

phrases.latin: nat lupus inter ovēs, fulvōs vehit unda leōnēs
phrases.english: the wolf swims among the sheep, the water carries tawny lions along

phrases.latin: Paulātim in aquam dēscende; ego tē teneō.
phrases.english: Get into the water slowly; I’ve got you.

phrases.latin: memor artificiī meī vetus frīgidae cultor mittō mē in mare
phrases.english: remembering my skill, an old devotee of cold water, I throw myself into the sea

phrases.latin: Nepōtēs et litterās et natāre aliaque rudīmenta per sē plērumque docuit
phrases.english: He taught his grandsons reading and swimming and the other first lessons himself, for the most part
